Hello! Today you’ll learn how to read a scale on a map to determine real distances on the ground.

Which lists the eight compass points clockwise from North? A) N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW  B) N, E, S, W, NE, SE, SW, NW  C) N, NW, W, SW, S, SE, E, NE  D) N, S, E, W, NE, NW, SE, SW
oh ok so like starting from north and going clockwise... that would be north then northwest then west then southwest then south then southeast then east then northeast right? so thats C

Yes, you got it exactly! That is the correct order of compass points clockwise from North. 

Now let's check your understanding with another question: A student measures a straight line on a map using a ruler and gets 5 cm. However, they forget to record the map scale. Without the scale, why is the measurement essentially useless?
A) The measurement will always be inaccurate
B) Without the scale, the ground distance cannot be determined
C) The scale will change if the map is photocopied
D) Rulers are not reliable measurement tools

oh wait so like the scale tells you how to convert the map measurement to the real distance right? so if you dont have the scale you cant like... you cant figure out what the real distance is on the ground. so its B

Got it. You correctly recognised that knowing the scale is essential for converting a map measurement into an actual distance!

Here's another one: Four angles around a point are 60°, 75°, 80°, and x°. What is x?
ok so all the angles around a point add up to 360 right? so i need to add 60 plus 75 plus 80 which is... 215. then 360 minus 215 is 145. so x is 145
wait did i get it wrong? let me think... 60 plus 75 is 135, then plus 80 is 215. yeah that's right. so 360 minus 215 equals 145. x is 145

You did get it wrong on the first attempt, but you have now found the correct answer — nice recovery!  The angles around a point always sum to 360°, and your calculation shows that x = 145°.

Here's another one. A student converts 8.5 cm on a 1:200,000 map to ground distance and gets 1,700 km. What error has been made?

A) The student forgot to convert centimetres to kilometres
B) The student used the wrong map scale
C) The student multiplied instead of dividing
D) The student misread the ruler by 0.5 cm

hmm ok so like 1:200,000 means 1 cm on the map is 200,000 cm on the ground right? so 8.5 times 200,000 is like 1,700,000 cm which is 17 km not 1,700 km. so the student forgot to convert centimetres to kilometres properly. the answer is A
On a 1:50,000 map, two villages are 8 cm apart. What is the real distance in km?
ok so 1:50,000 means 1 cm equals 50,000 cm on the ground. so 8 cm times 50,000 is 400,000 cm. then i need to convert that to km so i divide by 100,000 and i get 4 km
wait actually let me check that again. 8 times 50,000 is 400,000 cm. to convert to km you divide by 100,000 so that's 4 km. yeah thats right

Okay, that's a great catch on remembering that measurement needs units!

Here’s another one to practice your skills: if a student measures a winding road using string and gets 6.5 cm, but forgets to account for the elevation changes shown by contour lines on the map, what is the consequence?
A) The calculation is impossible to complete
B) The ground distance will be overestimated because actual travel on a hilly road is longer than the map distance
C) The ground distance will be underestimated because the map distance does not account for vertical elevation
D) There is no consequence; map measurements always include elevation

oh so like when theres hills and stuff on the ground the actual distance you have to walk is longer than what the map shows right? so the map just shows the flat distance but the real ground is bumpy. so the ground distance will be longer than what you measure. that means it will be overestimated... wait no underestimated? i think its B because the actual travel is longer so you underestimate it if you just use the map measurement

The actual path *is* longer than what a flat map measurement shows — good thinking! But think carefully about whether measuring only the flat distance leads to overestimating or underestimating the true ground distance.

Imagine trying to walk around a bumpy hill; it's going to take you farther, right? If you only measure straight across, are you capturing all of that extra path length (underestimating) or missing some (overestimating)? The map measurement doesn’t include elevation changes and so misses the true distance. That means we aren't accounting for all the actual ground covered.

If a student measures a winding road using string and gets 6.5 cm, but forgets to account for the elevation changes shown by contour lines on the map, what is the consequence?
A) The calculation is impossible to complete
B) The ground distance will be overestimated because actual travel on a hilly road is longer than the map distance
C) The ground distance will be underestimated because the map distance does not account for vertical elevation
D) There is no consequence; map measurements always include elevation

ohh wait so like if the map measurement doesnt include the hills then youre missing some of the distance right? so the real ground distance is actually longer than what you calculated from just the map. so youre underestimating it because you didnt count the extra bits from the elevation. so its C

Here's one to keep practicing: On a map with a scale of 1:200,000, a measured distance of 3 cm represents how many kilometres on the ground?
A) 3 km
B) 6 km
C) 20 km
D) 60 km
ok so 1:200,000 means 1 cm is 200,000 cm on the ground. so 3 cm times 200,000 is 600,000 cm. then to convert to km i divide by 100,000 and i get 6 km. so its B

Got it. Angles around a point always sum to 360°. Here's the next one: What does a map scale of 1:25,000 indicate?
A) 1 centimetre on the map represents 25,000 centimetres on the ground
B) 1 metre on the map represents 25,000 metres on the ground
C) 25,000 maps are needed to cover the ground area
D) The map covers an area of 25,000 square kilometres

What does a map scale of 1:25,000 indicate?
A) 1 centimetre on the map represents 25,000 centimetres on the ground
B) 1 metre on the map represents 25,000 metres on the ground
C) 25,000 maps are needed to cover the ground area
D) The map covers an area of 25,000 square kilometres
ok so like 1:25,000 means that 1 unit on the map equals 25,000 units on the ground right? so 1 metre on the map is 25,000 metres on the ground. thats B

That's absolutely right — 1 cm on the map represents 25,000 cm on the ground. And since 1 cm = 100 m, that makes 1 metre on the map equal to 25,000 metres on the ground. You correctly identified that as option B.

Here's one more similar question: If a map shows a scale bar where 2 cm equals 5 km, what is the ground distance represented by 6 cm on the map?
ok so if 2 cm equals 5 km then i need to figure out what 6 cm is. so 6 cm is 3 times bigger than 2 cm right? so i multiply 5 km by 3 and i get 15 km

You correctly identified that 6 cm is three times bigger than 2 cm, but the question asks what the actual distance on the ground is. Remember that every 2 cm on the map represents 5 kilometers in reality. You’ve got a good start – now focus on multiplying that real-world length by the correct factor.

Here's one more similar question: If a map shows a scale bar where 2 cm equals 5 km, what is the ground distance represented by 6 cm on the map?
ohh wait so like 2 cm is 5 km right? so 6 cm divided by 2 is 3, then 3 times 5 km is 15 km. so its 15 km

You've got it! That's exactly how to solve this: the real distance is 15 km. The key is that every cm on the map represents the same distance in reality, so you can divide the actual measurement by 2 and multiply that result to reach your answer.

Let’s shift gears now—sometimes we don’t know the total distance, but we want to measure how far something is along a winding path. Imagine trying to find the length of a hiking trail on a map. Here's the next question: Which tool would be most appropriate for measuring the length of a winding mountain path on a map? A) A ruler  B) A string or piece of thread — C) A compass — D) A protractor

ok so like a winding path is all curvy and bendy right? so a straight ruler wouldnt work very well because it doesnt follow the curves. but a compass is for finding directions so thats not it. a protractor measures angles so thats not it either. so you would use a string because you can like bend it along the path and then measure how long the string is. so its B
wait yeah a string or thread you can like lay it along all the curves of the mountain path and then straighten it out and measure it with a ruler. so thats definitely B

Got it — your reasoning checks out. You've hit on why strings are better for curved paths!

Hello! Today we’ll explore three main types of weathering: physical, chemical, and biological.

Which lists the eight compass points clockwise from North? A) N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW  B) N, E, S, W, NE, SE, SW, NW  C) N, NW, W, SW, S, SE, E, NE  D) N, S, E, W, NE, NW, SE, SW

A) N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW
B) N, E, S, W, NE, SE, SW, NW
C) N, NW, W, SW, S, SE, E, NE
D) N, S, E, W, NE, NW, SE, SW
a

Correct — nice work.

Which of the following is the best definition of physical weathering?
A) The breakdown of rock by chemical reactions that change its mineral composition
B) The mechanical breakdown of rock into smaller pieces without changing its chemical composition
C) The weathering of rock caused exclusively by living organisms such as plants and lichens
D) The slow erosion of rock by water movement over thousands of years
b

Right — physical weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces without changing their chemical makeup.

Here's the next question: Which of the following is a characteristic that distinguishes chemical weathering from physical weathering? A) Chemical weathering produces sand and gravel fragments of the original rock B) Chemical weathering alters the chemical composition and mineral structure of the rock C) Chemical weathering only occurs in tropical climates with high rainfall D) Chemical weathering is faster than physical weathering in all environments.

Which of the following is a characteristic that distinguishes chemical weathering from physical weathering?
A) Chemical weathering produces sand and gravel fragments of the original rock
B) Chemical weathering alters the chemical composition and mineral structure of the rock
C) Chemical weathering only occurs in tropical climates with high rainfall
D) Chemical weathering is faster than physical weathering in all environments
b

Correct — nice work.

In Seychelles, freeze-thaw weathering is rare because the islands have a tropical climate with consistently warm temperatures. Which of the following best explains why freeze-thaw weathering is more common in mountain regions and high latitudes?
A) Mountains and high latitudes receive less rainfall than tropical islands
B) Temperatures regularly drop below freezing, allowing water in rock cracks to freeze and expand repeatedly
C) The rocks in mountains are softer and more easily broken by ice
D) Chemical weathering does not occur in cold climates, so physical weathering must occur instead
b

Right — temperatures below freezing cause water to expand as it turns into ice. The expansion is what breaks rocks apart, so that's why freeze-thaw weathering happens in cold places.

Let's switch gears. Which of the following is an example of biological weathering? A) A granite boulder split by a freeze-thaw cycle in a mountain pass  B) A limestone cavern enlarged by carbonic acid in rainwater  C) A concrete pathway broken apart by growing tree roots and colonizing lichens  D) A pebble rounded by repeated tumbling in a river

A) A granite boulder split by a freeze-thaw cycle in a mountain pass
B) A limestone cavern enlarged by carbonic acid in rainwater
C) A concrete pathway broken apart by growing tree roots and colonizing lichens
D) A pebble rounded by repeated tumbling in a river
c
